overview: A four-week course for developers who already know Python or JavaScript and how to call a web API. Learners build real features on a large language model API, using the Claude API as the main example: messages and system prompts, prompt design for applications, structured outputs that code can trust, streaming, and tool use. Week 3 focuses on reliability and security (validation, prompt injection, small evaluation sets). Week 4 covers cost control and monitoring and the capstone: a deployed web app with structured outputs and a cost dashboard. The main path uses Python with Streamlit, and a Node.js with Next.js path is offered as extra code. The Claude API is a paid service, so the course shows a low-cost setup from the first day. Retrieval over documents is left to AI-15, and multi-step agents and automation workflows to AI-16.

time_plan.per_week: About 20 minutes of video, 120 minutes of building and testing code, and 40 minutes of reading documentation and quizzes. Week 4 goes mostly to the capstone app.

objectives.text: Describe how LLM APIs work: messages and roles, system prompts, tokens, context windows, stop reasons and key request settings such as max_tokens.
Explain how model choice, prompt design and token usage affect output quality, speed and cost.
Build LLM features that return schema-validated structured outputs and stream responses to a web interface.
Implement tool use (function calling) so that the model can request your own functions and APIs, with safe limits.
Diagnose failures such as invalid outputs, API errors, rate limits and prompt injection, and test prompts with a small evaluation set.
Choose and justify cost-control and production strategies (caching, batching, model choice, limits and monitoring) by weighing quality, speed and cost.
Ship a working AI-powered web app with structured outputs and a cost dashboard.

lessons.title: How LLM APIs Work
lessons.summary: The request and response cycle: a list of messages with user and assistant roles, an optional system prompt, and a response with text, a stop reason and token usage. The API is stateless, so your app sends the conversation history every time. Analogy: a very knowledgeable assistant who forgets every phone call unless you read the notes back.
lessons.exercise: Turn a 4-turn chat conversation into a messages list on paper, and mark which parts are sent again on the next request.

lessons.title: Setup: API Keys, SDKs and a Low-Cost Budget
lessons.summary: Creating an account and API key, storing the key in an environment variable (never in code or Git), and installing the official Python or TypeScript SDK. The Claude API is paid: set a monthly spend limit, use a smaller, cheaper model while developing, and keep max_tokens low. [VERSION] Console steps, SDK install, models and prices.
lessons.exercise: Make your first API call, then print the reply text, the stop reason and the input and output token counts.

lessons.title: Prompt Design for Applications
lessons.summary: Writing system prompts that set role, rules and output style; separating instructions from user data with clear tags; adding examples. Worked example: a reply assistant for a mobile network provider in Ghana. Prompts are code, so keep them in version control.
lessons.exercise: Improve a weak support-reply prompt in 3 versions and compare the outputs on the same 5 customer messages.

lessons.title: Tokens, Context and Cost
lessons.summary: Reading usage fields, counting tokens before sending, and estimating cost as tokens × price per million tokens. Longer context means more cost and slower replies. The same meaning can use different numbers of tokens in different languages. [VERSION] Prices and token-counting endpoint. [VERIFY] Language token differences.
lessons.exercise: Write a helper that logs tokens and estimated cost for every call, and compare the cost of the same request in English and one other language.

lessons.title: Structured Outputs with JSON Schemas
lessons.summary: Free text breaks code that needs fields. Defining a schema with Pydantic (Python) or Zod (TypeScript) and using the API's structured-output feature to get JSON that matches it. Worked example: extract supplier, date, total and currency from invoices from India, Mexico and Germany. [VERSION] Structured-output parameters and SDK helpers.
lessons.exercise: Build an invoice extractor that returns validated objects for 5 sample invoices written in different formats.

lessons.title: Validation, Errors and Retries
lessons.summary: Checking stop reasons (for example, output cut off by max_tokens or a refusal), handling API errors by type, and using the SDK's automatic retries for rate limits and server errors. Retrying a failed validation with the error message included. [VERSION] Error classes and retry defaults.
lessons.exercise: Add error handling to your extractor and test it with a too-small max_tokens value, an invalid key and a malformed input.

lessons.title: Streaming Responses
lessons.summary: Why streaming makes an app feel faster: users see text as it is generated. Using the SDK's streaming helpers and getting the final message and usage at the end. [VERSION] Streaming events and helpers.
lessons.exercise: Stream a long answer to the terminal, then record the time to the first token and the total time.

lessons.title: A Web Front End with Streamlit or Next.js
lessons.summary: Building a chat interface in Streamlit with chat input, session state for history and streamed output; the same pattern in Next.js as an extra. Keeping API keys in the host's secrets settings, and free hosting options. [VERSION] Streamlit functions and free hosting plans.
lessons.exercise: Build and deploy a small streaming chat app with a system prompt, and share the link with a classmate.

lessons.title: Tool Use: Letting the Model Call Your Functions
lessons.summary: Defining tools with a name, description and input schema. The model asks for a tool, your code runs it, and you send the result back. Analogy: a manager asks an assistant to check the stock system before replying to a customer. Worked example: a mock shipment-tracking tool for a courier company in Vietnam. [VERSION] Tool-definition options.
lessons.exercise: Add a tool that looks up an order status in a local dictionary, and test it with 5 customer questions.

lessons.title: Tool Loops and Guardrails
lessons.summary: Handling several tool calls in one turn, stopping after a maximum number of steps, strict schema checks on tool inputs, and asking a human to confirm any action that changes data. Give each tool the smallest permissions it needs.
lessons.exercise: Add a second tool that changes a delivery address, require user confirmation before it runs, and cap the loop at 5 steps.

lessons.title: Security: Prompt Injection and Data Privacy
lessons.summary: Any text from users, web pages or files can contain instructions that try to take control of the model. Separate instructions from data, limit what tools can do, and never place secrets in prompts. Send only the personal data you need; data protection laws differ by country. [REGION] [VERIFY]
lessons.exercise: Attack your own app with 5 prompt-injection attempts, record which ones worked, and fix at least 2.

lessons.title: Testing Prompts with a Small Evaluation Set
lessons.summary: A set of 20–30 test inputs with expected properties. Automatic checks (valid schema, required fields, length) and careful use of a model as a judge. Comparing prompt versions and catching regressions before users do.
lessons.exercise: Build a 20-case test set for your extractor, run 2 prompt versions, and report the pass rate and cost of each.

modules.title: Production, Cost Control and the Capstone

lessons.title: Cost Control in Practice
lessons.summary: The main levers: prompt caching for repeated context, batch processing for jobs that can wait, sending easy tasks to a smaller model, output limits and per-user quotas. Measuring quality before and after each change. [VERSION] Caching and batch features, discounts and rules.
lessons.exercise: Apply prompt caching to a request with a long system prompt, and compare the cached and uncached token usage and cost.

lessons.title: Capstone Step 1: Build the Core Feature
lessons.summary: Choosing a use case, for example a job-advert analyser for a recruitment agency in Poland or a meal planner for a grocery app in Nigeria. Writing a one-page spec, then building the core feature with structured outputs and, if useful, a tool.
lessons.exercise: Capstone step 1: write the spec and build the core feature with a validated schema and streaming output.

lessons.title: Capstone Step 2: Usage Logging and a Cost Dashboard
lessons.summary: Logging every call (time, feature, model, tokens, latency, estimated cost, errors) to SQLite or CSV. Building a dashboard page with cost per day, cost per request and error rate, and an alert when spend nears a limit.
lessons.exercise: Capstone step 2: add usage logging and a cost dashboard page to your app.

lessons.title: Capstone Step 3: Test, Deploy and Present
lessons.summary: A final checklist: run the evaluation set and injection tests, set spend limits, deploy to a free hosting plan, and write a README with architecture, cost per request and known limits. Presenting the app in a 3-minute demo.
lessons.exercise: Capstone step 3: deploy the app, share the link and README, and record a 3-minute demo.

capstone.title: AI-Powered Web App with a Cost Dashboard
capstone.brief: Ship a working AI-powered web app with structured outputs and a cost dashboard. Learners design and deploy a small web app that uses an LLM API with validated structured outputs, streaming and optional tool use, log every call, and show usage and cost on a dashboard page.
